bp: A sequential recommender watches the ordered trail of things a person touched and tries to choose the next useful item from a very large catalog. Training such a system usually needs both positive examples, such as the item the user actually chose, and negative examples, meaning items the user probably did not want at that moment. The positive side is visible in the log. The negative side is mostly guessed, because a user did not inspect every movie, beauty product, or beer before choosing one. This paper serves that hidden training problem. It asks how to pick useful negative items without accidentally telling the model that a genuinely attractive but unclicked item is bad. CATS treats the item catalog as having an internal neighborhood structure. Instead of drawing negatives blindly, it uses item clusters and a trial-and-learning choice rule to decide where negatives should come from during training.
wh: The hard part is that an unchosen item is not automatically a bad item. In a huge catalog, most items were never shown, never noticed, or simply not reached in that session. If training labels many of them as negative, the model may learn from guesses rather than facts. Random sampling can pick easy negatives that teach almost nothing, such as comparing a horror movie preference against an unrelated kitchen item. Popularity-based sampling can overexpose already common items and make the model inherit popularity bias. Hard-negative mining tries to choose difficult confusable items, but that creates another danger: the hardest nearby item may be something the user would actually like, so it becomes a false negative. Sequential recommendation makes this worse because the user's current intent changes over time. A useful negative must be close enough to sharpen the boundary, but not so close that it is probably another acceptable next item.
naive: A smart beginner might train the recommender by pairing each clicked item with a few randomly chosen unclicked items. That is simple, cheap, and seems fair because every catalog item has a chance to be selected. The failure is that random negatives are often too obvious. If the positive item is a face cream, a random beer or unrelated product may only teach the model a coarse category split. Another beginner might choose popular items as negatives, but then the training process keeps returning to the same crowded part of the catalog and can strengthen popularity bias. A third attempt is to choose items that the model currently finds confusing. That can help, but if the confusing item sits right beside the positive item in taste or purpose, it may be a false negative.
ap: The core idea of CATS is to use the catalog's learned neighborhoods as a guide for risk. The abstract says false negatives tend to lie in the same cluster as the positive item, while true hard negatives are more likely to be found in nearby clusters. In plain terms, items in the exact same group may be substitutes the user could have liked, so treating them as bad is dangerous. Items in neighboring groups are still similar enough to be challenging, but are less likely to be another hidden positive. CATS therefore samples from three regions: the positive item's own cluster, neighboring clusters, and the rest of the item space. It adapts that mixture over time with Thompson Sampling, a probability-based trial rule that favors sources that have looked useful while still testing uncertain sources. It also lowers the chance of sampling from the positive cluster as training proceeds.
mech: The mechanism begins with interaction sequences and an item catalog. A sequential recommendation model such as SASRec, BERT4Rec, or BSARec needs training cases: a user's recent item history, the next item actually observed, and selected negative items used for comparison. Before sampling negatives, CATS groups items without manual labels. This unsupervised clustering step builds neighborhoods from item representations, meaning compact numeric descriptions learned from item evidence; the important assumption is that nearby descriptions reflect related user preference. For a given positive item, CATS identifies three candidate regions. The first is the item's own cluster. The second is the set of nearest clusters, which are close but not identical neighborhoods. The third is the remaining item space. During training, the sampler chooses which region to draw from. Thompson Sampling supplies this choice rule: it keeps uncertainty about how useful each region is, samples from that uncertainty, and therefore balances using the region that seems best with continuing to test alternatives. After a region is chosen, a negative item is drawn from it and used in the recommender's training comparison. Over time, CATS decays the probability of sampling from the positive item's own cluster. The output is not a new recommender architecture, but a different stream of negative training examples that can be plugged into several sequential models.
math: The first mathematical idea is similarity as a learned map. Each item is placed into a compact description, and clustering groups items that are near one another on that map. Clustering is useful here because the catalog is too large to reason about item by item, but the grouping is also risky because closeness compresses many details into a few numbers. CATS uses that compression carefully: same-cluster items are treated as high false-negative risk, nearest-cluster items as likely useful hard negatives, and far-away items as safer but often less informative. The second idea is probability under uncertainty. Thompson Sampling is a repeated-choice rule for situations where the system does not know which option will pay off best. Rather than always choosing the currently best-looking source of negatives, it samples from its current belief about each source, so uncertain but promising regions can still be explored. The third idea is an exploration-versus-exploitation tradeoff. Exploration tests different negative regions; exploitation uses the region that appears to train the model well. The decay schedule adds a time-shaped assumption: early same-cluster sampling may give useful difficulty, but later it can accumulate false negatives, so its weight should shrink.
dots: This paper sits inside the repo's recommender-systems family, where the shared pressure is choosing a small useful set from a huge item pile with partial evidence. CATS works one step before final ranking: it repairs the training comparisons that teach the recommender what should be placed above what. It connects to sequence modeling because the recommender being trained reads ordered user histories, so a negative item is judged relative to a changing current intent, not a static user profile. It connects to similarity because clusters decide which items are close enough to be dangerous substitutes and which neighboring items are useful challengers. It connects to probability because Thompson Sampling makes the sampler act while uncertain about which region supplies the best negatives. Compared with other recommendation papers in the repo that handle cold start, long histories, item identifiers, or on-device cost, this one focuses on the quieter source of error inside training: the guessed examples of what the user did not want.
ww: CATS should work better than naive sampling because it separates two kinds of closeness that ordinary hard-negative mining can blur. A negative that is completely unrelated may be safe, but it does not teach the model a sharp preference boundary. A negative inside the positive item's own cluster may be sharp, but it may also be an item the user would have accepted if shown. A neighboring cluster is a useful middle ground: similar enough to make the model compare carefully, but less likely to be the same hidden preference. The adaptive bandit rule helps because the best source of negatives need not be fixed throughout training. Early on, the model may need broad and sometimes close comparisons to learn catalog structure. Later, repeated same-cluster negatives can become harmful if they keep marking possible positives as bad. By reducing positive-cluster sampling over time, CATS tries to keep the early teaching value while lowering the long-run risk. The reported gains across three sequential models support the claim that the sampling policy, not only the model architecture, changes recommendation quality.
po: The payoff is a better way to train sequential recommenders over very large item collections without checking every possible item. The abstract reports that CATS consistently beats standard and advanced negative-sampling baselines when used with SASRec, BERT4Rec, and BSARec on MovieLens-1M, Amazon Beauty, and BeerAdvocate. It also reports improvements above 20 percent in NDCG@10 over vanilla sampling and above 16 percent over more advanced methods. In practical terms, the method buys cleaner training pressure: the recommender sees negatives that are informative enough to improve ranking, while reducing the chance that appealing unobserved items are repeatedly mislabeled as unwanted.
limits: The method depends on the item clusters being meaningful for preference. If the learned item map groups items by a surface property that does not match what users care about, same-cluster and neighboring-cluster risk will be misread. The abstract states the key belief about false negatives and nearest clusters, but that belief may vary by catalog, domain, and how item representations are built. CATS also assumes the adaptive sampling feedback reflects better training rather than a temporary fit to the chosen datasets or models. The evaluation covers three datasets and three sequential recommenders, which is useful evidence, but it does not prove the same behavior for every catalog size, exposure policy, user group, or production feedback loop.
